payload.text: Most of what archaeologists know about ancient trade comes from rubbish: broken pots, kitchen bones and the seeds that fell between floorboards. Treasure tells a thinner story, because valuables were mended, melted and passed on, while a cracked jar was simply {{b1}} where it lay. Waste is also honest about quantity, since a single kitchen heap can show that oil arrived from three provinces, which no inscription would ever trouble to {{b2}}. The difficulty is that rubbish survives only where the ground is {{b3}} or dry enough to halt bacteria, so the map of what we know follows soil chemistry rather than the real {{b4}} of ancient life.

gaps.explanation: take the blame（責任・非を引き受ける）が定型表現。catch は「捕まえる」で blame とは組まない。hold は hold someone responsible の形なら使えるが hold the blame とは言わない。bring も bring a charge against ~ のように使い、bring the blame とはしない。

payload.title: The Night Train Comes Back
paragraphs: For about thirty years the sleeper train looked like a museum piece. Budget airlines undercut it on price, new high-speed lines beat it between capitals close enough to reach before lunch, and the carriages themselves were the least profitable stock an operator could own: heavy, slow to clean, and standing still for most of every day. Between 2000 and 2016 one European network after another quietly withdrew them, and the services that survived did so on scenic routes where the journey, rather than the destination, was the point.

The revival that followed was not driven by nostalgia. An Austrian operator bought the discarded carriages of a larger neighbour, rebuilt them, and ran the night train as an ordinary business, adding routes when the bookings justified it and dropping them when they did not. Passengers were doing their own arithmetic in the meantime: a berth from Vienna to Brussels saves a night's hotel as well as a flight, and it removes two airport transfers, two security queues and a whole day from the calendar.

The obstacles now are administrative rather than commercial. Charges for using the track are set country by country and can double the cost of crossing three borders; safety rules for sleeping passengers differ from state to state; and a carriage approved in one country may sit unused for a year while a neighbouring authority examines it. None of that is beyond the reach of policy, which is why the operators keep saying that what they want is not subsidy but a single set of rules.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Night trains were withdrawn as unprofitable, but have returned on straightforwardly commercial grounds, and what limits them now is a patchwork of national regulation rather than weak demand.
Sleeper services can survive only where governments are willing to pay for them, since no operator has ever run one at a profit.
Budget airlines have lost so many passengers to the railways that several of them have withdrawn from short European routes.
Older travellers' affection for the sleeping car has persuaded operators to restore services that make no financial sense.

questions.after: unlike the trains that used the same lines by day.

could not be fitted with the safety equipment that new rules demanded

questions.prompt: 夜行列車が乗客にとって費用の面で有利になる理由を最もよく表している語句はどれですか。

questions.prompt: 筆者が本文全体で最も伝えたいことはどれですか。
options: Written off as unprofitable relics, sleeper trains have been brought back by an operator running them on commercial terms and by passengers who count hotel nights and airport time, so the remaining barrier is Europe's mismatched national rules rather than a shortage of demand.
Because high-speed lines now link most European capitals, the night train can only ever serve tourists travelling for the scenery.
The main lesson of the sleeper's return is that heavy old carriages should be scrapped and replaced with newly built ones as soon as funds allow.
Track charges are so high across Europe that no cross-border rail service can be expected to survive without public money.

payload.title: The Shop That Only Fixes Things
paragraphs: A repair cafe is a simple idea: a hall, a few tables, volunteers who own tools, and anybody who turns up carrying something broken. Nothing is sold and nothing is charged for, which keeps the whole event outside the rules that govern a shop. The first was held in Amsterdam in 2009, and there are now several thousand around the world. The same three items dominate every log book: lamps, vacuum cleaners, and the cheaper sort of headphones.

The movement's own figures are modest and honestly reported, since rather more than half of what comes through the door leaves working. The failures are the instructive part. A volunteer can usually fit a new switch or a new cable, but is stopped by a glued case, a screw with an unfamiliar head, or a component that the manufacturer sells only to approved workshops, if it sells it at all. Most of what defeats a repair cafe was decided years earlier at a drawing board.

That is the argument which has carried the idea into law. Several governments now require makers of household machines to supply spare parts for a decade and to publish repair manuals, and a few have cut the tax charged on repair work. The cafes themselves will never handle much of a country's waste. What they produce is evidence, in the form of a queue of ordinary objects that could have been mended, photographed and counted, and evidence is what committees respond to.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Volunteer repair events mend a fair share of what they receive, but their real contribution is the evidence they gather that design choices, not owners' carelessness, make many goods unrepairable.
Repair cafes have grown so quickly that they now divert a significant proportion of household waste from landfill.
The chief obstacle facing repair cafes is a shortage of volunteers with the skills to work on modern electrical goods.
Because manufacturers have begun publishing repair manuals, the work of repair cafes is largely finished.

questions.after: for any of the work that its volunteers do.

spans.text: a hall, a few tables, volunteers who own tools

questions.sentence: Success rates, in other words, say more about manufacturers than about volunteers.

questions.prompt: 筆者が本文全体で最も伝えたいことはどれですか。
options: Free volunteer workshops repair over half of the goods brought to them, and the ones they cannot save expose glued cases and withheld parts, so their lasting effect has been to supply lawmakers with the evidence behind spare-part and manual requirements.
Repair cafes have proved that most broken household goods can be mended by anyone who is given a screwdriver and a little patience.

Since the cafes handle only a tiny share of household waste, their influence on manufacturers and governments has been negligible.
